title: Apex security and API-version defaults
summary: Separate class sharing context from database access mode and verify security when changing an Apex API version.
prerequisites: M01–M05: CRUD, FLS, record access, and restrictions.
Apex classes, SOQL, DML, and test users.
learningObjectives: Distinguish record-sharing context from operation access mode.
Write explicit-mode comparisons and negative tests.

sections.heading: Understand the mechanism
body: Apex security questions become easier when you name two separate decisions. The class sharing declaration describes record-sharing behavior in the relevant execution context. A database operation's access mode determines whether it enforces user-level permissions or deliberately runs with elevated behavior. Saying only 'this class is with sharing' does not explain every field or object check.

Defaults are versioned. In API 67.0 and later, classes without an explicit sharing declaration default to with sharing, and database operations default to user mode. In older versions, omission of a sharing declaration preserves the current sharing context rather than being a synonym for an explicit without sharing declaration; older database operations default to system mode. Read the current reference when migrating an existing class.

An explicitly user-mode query applies the running user's record access, object permissions, and field-level security. If a required field is inaccessible, the operation can fail rather than silently returning a sanitized response. Decide whether the product needs a clear error or an intentionally reduced response, and implement that choice. Do not catch every security error and return an empty list that looks like a legitimate absence of records.

System mode is not a shortcut for fixing permission errors. Some backend operations legitimately require privileges, but their entry point, allowed records, inputs, and output must be constrained. In system mode, the calling class's sharing declaration remains relevant to record-level behavior. Trigger context has its own rules; an API 67+ user-mode database operation still enforces its user-mode requirements even inside a trigger.

callouts.text: Review sharing context and database operation mode separately, and include the class API version in the review.

sections.heading: Northstar Motors worked example
body: Anna owns TD-A, while Max owns a private TD-B. Remove Anna's field Read for a field selected by the experiment. Compare an explicit user-mode query with a separately justified system-mode version, using the same identity and data. A correct result is not necessarily a row count: the user-mode operation may reject inaccessible fields before returning results.

Then compare copies of the small class compiled at API 66.0 and 68.0 with omitted declarations or modes. Record the actual differences without changing the data or persona. This is a migration experiment, not permission advice. The final application should state critical security choices explicitly so that intent is visible during review.

callouts.text: Does with sharing alone prove that every returned field is readable to Anna?

codeBlocks.caption: Query fragment: explicit user-mode read of starter fields

sections.heading: Build and inspect
body: Use existing starter fields. Keep comparison classes separate and record their .cls-meta.xml API versions. Do not deploy experimental privileged endpoints to a shared or production environment.

steps.title: Prepare the security matrix
steps.instruction: Define visible/hidden records and readable/hidden fields for a restricted user. Ensure the administrator can create fixtures without being used as the test persona.
steps.expected: The matrix predicts both rows and field-related failures.

steps.title: Run explicit-mode comparisons
steps.instruction: Execute the same selected fields and filters with clearly stated class context and operation mode. Capture success or the specific access failure.
steps.expected: Results can be explained without relying on an ambiguous default.

steps.title: Evaluate a version upgrade
steps.instruction: Run the controlled API 66/68 comparison, then make critical declarations explicit and repeat the intended application tests.
steps.expected: The change is reviewed as a behavior change, not merely an XML edit.

sections.heading: Failure cases and boundaries
body: An administrator test can conceal FLS defects. System.runAs changes the test identity, but it does not by itself turn every system-mode database operation into a user-mode operation.
Returning raw exception messages can reveal implementation details. Report an appropriate user-facing error while preserving a safe diagnostic reference for the developer.

callouts.text: Never teach 'Apex always runs in system mode' as an unversioned rule for current Salesforce.

exercise.title: Produce an Apex security comparison
exercise.brief: Explain and verify one read path under explicit modes and API-version defaults.
steps: Write the final explicit policy and negative tests.
acceptance: The report separates sharing from CRUD/FLS.
No broad permission is added solely to make the test green.
exercise.stretch: Explain one limitation and propose a small follow-up experiment before extending the implementation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Is omitted sharing always without sharing?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. Older omission preserves context; API 67+ defaults to with sharing.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does user mode change?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It enforces the user's permissions and sharing for that database operation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why review an API-version upgrade?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Versioned defaults can change data access and failures even when the business code is unchanged.

recap: Prove behavior under a restricted identity.
